summary: Defines cryptographic transforms based on Russian GOST algorithms for use in IKEv2, covering transforms beyond the ciphers already addressed in RFC 9227. It exists to help implementations that need GOST support.

eli5.summary: IPsec's key setup normally uses certain codes. This adds more of the codes from Russian standards.

questions: how to use russian crypto with ipsec
how to use gost with ikev2
what gost algorithms does ikev2 support
subtitle: Using Russian cryptographic standards in IPsec key exchange.

tldr.problem: IPsec's key exchange protocol IKEv2 has traditionally used Western cryptographic algorithms. Some countries and organizations require or prefer GOST algorithms, which are Russian cryptographic standards, but IKEv2 did not define how to use them for all its cryptographic functions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9385 defines new cryptographic transforms for IKEv2 based on GOST algorithms. These include the Streebog hash functions, GOST signature algorithms, and GOST key exchange methods on twisted Edwards curves, allowing IKEv2 to use these ciphers alongside the encryption ciphers already specified in RFC 9227.
tldr.outcome: Implementations and networks that need to comply with GOST-based security policies can now run IKEv2 entirely using Russian cryptographic standards. This improves interoperability for such deployments and supports regulatory requirements in regions that mandate or prefer GOST.

today: RFC 9385 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It complements RFC 9227 to provide comprehensive GOST support for IKEv2 implementations. Networks and implementations that require GOST algorithms can use these transforms for IPsec deployments.

sections.title: GOST Algorithms for IKEv2
sections.content:
GOST refers to Russian cryptographic standard algorithms. The abbreviation stands for the Russian words for "State Standard". These include cipher families, hash functions, and digital signature algorithms. RFC 9227 already defined how to use the GOST block ciphers Kuznyechik and Magma (which use MGM mode) for encrypting IKE Security Associations. RFC 9385 extends this by defining additional GOST-based transforms for IKEv2's pseudorandom function, key exchange, and digital signature authentication.

The protocol operates within the framework of IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2), which is a core part of IPsec. IKEv2 is responsible for authenticating peers and agreeing upon encryption keys used to protect data traffic in a Virtual Private Network (VPN) or other IPsec deployment. Without these new definitions, implementers who wished to support GOST algorithms had no standard way to integrate them into the full IKEv2 protocol.
sections.eli5: IKEv2 is the part of VPN that makes two computers agree on secret keys. It normally uses certain math tricks, but Russia has its own official math tricks. This document explains how to do IKEv2 the Russian way.

sections.title: GOST Cryptographic Components
sections.content:
RFC 9385 defines four main categories of cryptographic transforms:

Encryption: RFC 9227 already covered this, defining how to use Kuznyechik and Magma ciphers in MGM (Multilinear Galois Mode) for IKE SA protection.

Pseudorandom Function (PRF): A new transform, PRF_HMAC_STREEBOG_512, uses the GOST R 34.11-2012 hash function (also known as Streebog) in HMAC construction. Streebog has two variants: a 256-bit output version for use with 256-bit curves and a 512-bit output version for use with 512-bit curves. The PRF is used to derive keying material from the shared secret in IKEv2.

Key Exchange: Two new transforms use the GOST R 34.10-2012 elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman algorithm on twisted Edwards curves. One uses the 256-bit curve (GOST3410_2012_256, transform ID 33), and the other uses the 512-bit curve (GOST3410_2012_512, transform ID 34). Both sides select a private key, derive their public key, exchange them, and compute a shared secret from the x coordinate of a point on the curve.

Authentication: The GOST R 34.10-2012 digital signature algorithm is used for IKE SA authentication. It produces a signature consisting of two integers, r and s, each either 256 or 512 bits depending on the curve. Two hash functions are defined: STREEBOG_256 (hash ID 6) for use with the 256-bit signature algorithm and STREEBOG_512 (hash ID 7) for use with the 512-bit variant.
sections.eli5: There are several pieces: a PRF (a function that makes random keys), a way to swap keys between computers (key exchange), and a way to prove who you are (signatures). GOST versions of all of these are now defined.

sections.title: IKE SA Establishment with GOST
sections.content:
An IKEv2 exchange using GOST transforms follows the standard IKEv2 two-exchange process: IKE_SA_INIT, which establishes a temporary security association and negotiates algorithms, and IKE_AUTH, which performs mutual authentication and creates the IPsec SAs for protecting data traffic.

During IKE_SA_INIT, both sides advertise the transforms they support, including the new GOST transforms. Both sides select a shared ciphersuite—for example, one that uses GOST3410_2012_256 for key exchange, HMAC_STREEBOG_512 for the PRF, and Kuznyechik in MGM mode for IKE SA encryption.

In the key exchange step, the initiator sends its public key Q_i computed as d_i * G, where d_i is the private key and G is the curve generator. The responder computes its public key Q_r and sends it back. Both sides then compute the shared secret S = ((m / q) * d_i) * Q_r = ((m / q) * d_r) * Q_i, where m is the group order and q is the subgroup order. The shared secret K is taken as the x coordinate of S in little-endian representation. The size is either 256 or 512 bits.

During IKE_AUTH, if digital signature authentication is used, the initiator sends a signature computed using the GOST algorithm over the handshake transcript. Both sides must verify that the public key received is actually a point on the curve and that the computed point S is not the identity element. These checks are mandatory to prevent attacks.
sections.eli5: Two computers use GOST math to agree on a secret number, then use that number to encrypt their communication and to prove to each other that they are who they say they are.

sections.title: Deployment and Compatibility
sections.content:
RFC 9385 is an Informational RFC that does not require any changes to the IKEv2 protocol itself. Implementations that wish to support GOST transforms can do so by adding code that implements the new transforms and negotiates them via the standard IKEv2 mechanism.

A GOST IKEv2 deployment typically involves selecting appropriate parameter sets from RFC 7836, which defines the curve parameters and other details for GOST algorithms. For example, the 256-bit GOST key exchange uses the id-tc26-gost-3410-2012-256-paramSetA parameter set, and the 512-bit variant uses id-tc26-gost-3410-2012-512-paramSetC.

Implementations must check that received public keys are valid points on the selected curve and that they are not the identity element. Failure to do so can lead to security vulnerabilities. The specification includes test vectors in Appendix A to help implementations validate their code.

Interoperability is achieved through standard negotiation: both peers offer the transforms they support, and they select a common ciphersuite. Peers that do not support GOST can negotiate traditional algorithms like AES or SHA-256 instead.
sections.eli5: Implementations add GOST support as an optional feature. Networks that need GOST can use it, and those that do not can keep using the old codes.

sections.title: Security and Validation Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 9385 emphasizes several mandatory security checks. When receiving a GOST public key in the Key Exchange payload, the peer must verify that it is actually a point on the chosen curve. It must also check that the computed shared secret point S is not the identity element of the curve. If either check fails, the exchange must be aborted, and the INVALID_SYNTAX notification MAY be sent.

The specification does not introduce new authentication methods; existing IKEv2 authentication methods like "Shared Key Message Integrity Code", "NULL Authentication", and "Digital Signature" (RFC 7427) can be used with GOST algorithms without modification. The AUTH payload content calculation remains the same; only the hash function and signature algorithm change.

The security of the GOST elliptic curves and the Streebog hash functions is discussed in external documents cited in the RFC. Some research has identified preimage attacks on Streebog under certain conditions, but these are not considered practical attacks for the use cases covered by this RFC.
sections.eli5: The math only works if both sides follow the rules, especially checking that received numbers are real points on the curve and not fake or degenerate ones.

sections.title: Use and Status
sections.content:
RFC 9385 is published in the Independent Submissions Stream and is Informational. It represents a standardization effort by the Russian Standardisation Technical Committee on Cryptographic Information Protection, documented in [GOST-IKEv2]. The RFC does not imply IETF endorsement of GOST algorithms themselves, only standardization of how to use them in IKEv2 for those implementations that choose to support them.

The specification is intended for implementations and deployments that must or prefer to use GOST algorithms due to regulatory requirements or organizational policy. It facilitates interoperability among GOST-aware IKEv2 implementations and allows such deployments to participate in standardized VPNs alongside other IPsec-based systems.

The RFC is stable and has not been obsoleted. The transforms defined here can be combined with encryption algorithms from RFC 9227 to create complete IKEv2 ciphersuites that meet various GOST requirements.
sections.eli5: This document lets IKEv2 implementations add GOST support if they need to. It is stable and not changing.
